newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets pause for breath but may fall again soon.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets pause for breath but may fall again soon.

text.p: World oil prices drew breath on Monday after plunging nearly nine percent last week to nine month lows.
Dealers said further losses were likely in the short term as global oil supplies grow strongly.
London futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude ended up 10 cents at $17.78 a barrel for May, barely denting last week's $1.70 slide and dwarfed by losses of $6.50 so far this year.
"Something fairly spectacular has to take place to dramatically improve crude fundamentals. There is still too much supply around," said brokers GNI in a report.
Cheap crude oil has encouraged refiners to process more oil ahead of the peak summer gasoline season, taking advantage of profit margins which have not been seen for nearly a year.
But industry sources say the boot remains firmly on the buyers' foot, partly because of ample supply from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

"It seems to me that OPEC (members) are sticking to the extra production they enjoyed due to very firm prices last year despite the fact that the market has become one of surplus rather than shortage," said the head of crude trading for a major North Sea producer.
OPEC's 11 producers lifted output by 130,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 26.90 million bpd in March, almost 1.9 million bpd above their official ceiling.
This has played a large part in driving prices down to nine-month lows and destroying any hopes that they might have harboured of a repeat of last year's windfall revenues, analysts said.

Iraqi exports under a United Nations oil-for-food deal, due for renewal in June shortly before the cartel's regular ministerial meeting in Vienna, may rise in May as falling benchmark prices force Baghdad to ship greater volumes to meet its $1 billion target.

"The lower the price goes, the more Iraq can pump, creating a vicious circle which OPEC will have to tackle at its June meeting if it doesn't want to see even weaker prices," said the senior North Sea trader.

But with most OPEC members apparently consigning quota compliance to the dustbin and non-OPEC output continuing to grow at a rapid rate, industry sources expect even weaker prices, at least for the near future.
In the longer term rising Asian demand could stem the slide, some analysts say, pointing to forward crude derivatives which are pricing Brent around current levels for the next two years.
"Clearly there is a battle between OPEC output, which is a mixture of cheating and Iraq, and the demand driver out of the Far East," said Paul Spedding, oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
"The OPEC hare is winning the race at the moment but the super-charged Far East tortoise is catching up fast," he said.

Last month, the Japanese Trade Ministry said Asian demand for oil products should outpace the region's refining capacity by the year 2000, with annual growth reaching at least 5.1 percent, more than double the global forecast.
